<reason>A's core mechanism — per-crash lethality from mass and front-end geometry — was never dented; B attacked trend attribution and instruments instead. A answered both pressure questions directly, turned B's five-year timing frame (redesigns are slow too; curb fees bite day one via trip choice; fleet-wide protection beats corner-by-corner), and the closing defused B's best late points: parking/curb fees are exposure-based, and price signals deter without earmarks. B's strongest line — the motion names a body-style category, and A's "yes" to the three-ton sedan question required off-motion apparatus — was a genuine hit, but A anchored itself in the motion's own when-clause ("when their size imposes higher costs"), which B never engaged head-on, and B conceded cost-keyed pricing is acceptable in principle, shrinking the objection to drafting. B's alternatives crumbled: design standards were abandoned after A's authority attack, length-metering concedes a size-keyed curb fee, and redesigns need the fee's revenue. B was rhetorically superb but dropped too many late threads.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Q1 forcing A's "yes" on the cost-equivalent sedan, converted in B4.5 into "every time PRO defends the policy, they describe a different one" — the sharpest catch of the debate. A contained it via the motion's when-clause and B's own concession, but the decisive unresolved exchange was A's A2: redesigns need the fee's revenue, are equally slow, and protect one corner while a smaller fleet protects every corner — B never answered that comparison.</best_rebuttal>
